subject: probability
title: Single Fair Coin Toss
prompt: A fair coin is tossed once. What is the probability of getting heads?
solution: A fair coin has two possible outcomes: Heads and Tails. Because the coin is fair, each outcome is equally likely. Therefore, the probability of getting Heads is the number of favorable outcomes (1) divided by the total number of possible outcomes (2). Hence, P(Heads) = 1 / 2 = 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Two Heads from Two Coins
prompt: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting two heads?
solution: When two fair coins are tossed, the sample space consists of four equally likely outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Only one of these outcomes (HH) corresponds to getting two heads. Therefore, the probability is 1 favorable outcome divided by 4 total outcomes, giving P = 1 / 4 = 0.25.

subject: probability
title: Drawing an Ace
prompt: A card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability the card is an Ace?
solution: A standard deck contains 52 cards, of which exactly 4 are Aces. Since each card is equally likely to be drawn, the probability of drawing an Ace is the ratio of favorable outcomes (4 Aces) to total possible outcomes (52 cards). Thus, P(Ace) = 4 / 52 = 1 / 13 ≈ 0.076923.

subject: probability
title: Two Aces Without Replacement
prompt: Two cards are drawn from a deck without replacement. What is the probability both are Aces?
solution: On the first draw, the probability of getting an Ace is 4 / 52. After one Ace has been drawn, only 3 Aces remain out of 51 cards. Therefore, the probability the second card is also an Ace is 3 / 51. Because the second draw depends on the first, we multiply these probabilities: (4 / 52) × (3 / 51) = 12 / 2652 ≈ 0.004524.

subject: probability
title: Choosing the Correct Exit
prompt: A drunk passenger randomly chooses one of 3 exits at a station. What is the probability he chooses the correct exit?
solution: There are 3 exits, and the passenger selects one at random. Each exit has an equal chance of being chosen. Only one of the three exits is correct. Therefore, the probability of choosing the correct exit is 1 favorable choice divided by 3 possible choices: P = 1 / 3 ≈ 0.333333.

subject: probability
title: Union via Inclusion-Exclusion
prompt: Two events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.7, P(B) = 0.5, and P(A ∩ B) = 0.4. What is P(A ∪ B)?
solution: To compute the probability of at least one of the events occurring, we use the inclusion–exclusion principle: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). Substituting the given values gives 0.7 + 0.5 − 0.4 = 0.8. This subtraction avoids double-counting the overlap between A and B.

subject: probability
title: Intersection of Independent Events
prompt: Events A and B are independent. If P(A) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.6, what is P(A ∩ B)?
solution: For independent events, the occurrence of one event does not affect the probability of the other. By definition of independence, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B). Substituting the values gives 0.2 × 0.6 = 0.12.

subject: probability
title: Complement Rule
prompt: If P(A) = 0.4, what is P(Aᶜ)?
solution: The complement of an event A, denoted Aᶜ, represents all outcomes in which A does not occur. Since total probability is 1, we use the complement rule: P(Aᶜ) = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.4 = 0.6.

subject: probability
title: Axioms of Probability
prompt: Which of the following must be true for any probability P(A)?
solution: By the axioms of probability, the probability of any event must lie between 0 and 1 inclusive. Values outside this range would violate the fundamental definition of probability.

subject: probability
title: Exactly Two Heads in Three Tosses
prompt: Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of exactly two heads?
solution: With three fair coins, there are 2³ = 8 equally likely outcomes. Exactly two heads can occur in three ways: HHT, HTH, and THH. Therefore, the probability is 3 favorable outcomes divided by 8 total outcomes: 3 / 8 = 0.375.

subject: probability
title: Uniform Interval Probability
prompt: A point is chosen uniformly on the interval [0, 1]. What is the probability it lies between 0.2 and 0.6?
solution: For a uniform distribution on [0,1], probability is proportional to length. The interval from 0.2 to 0.6 has length 0.6 − 0.2 = 0.4. Since the total interval length is 1, the probability is 0.4.

subject: probability
title: Two Random Numbers Close Together
prompt: Two people independently choose a random number in [0,1]. What is the probability their numbers differ by less than 0.1?
solution: Geometrically, this corresponds to the region in the unit square where |x − y| < 0.1. The excluded area consists of two triangles of side length 0.9, whose combined area is 0.9² = 0.81. Therefore, the favorable area is 1 − 0.81 = 0.19.

subject: probability
title: Four Points in a Semicircle
prompt: Four points are randomly placed on a circle. What is the probability they all lie within some semicircle?
solution: A classical result states that for N points placed independently and uniformly on a circle, the probability that all lie within some semicircle is N / 2^(N−1). Substituting N = 4 gives 4 / 8 = 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Conditional Probability from a Joint
prompt: If P(A) = 0.3 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.15, what is P(B|A)?
solution: Conditional probability measures the chance of B occurring given that A has occurred. By definition, P(B|A) = P(A ∩ B) / P(A). Substituting the given values yields 0.15 / 0.3 = 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Die Roll of at Least Four
prompt: A die is rolled. What is the probability the number is at least 4?
solution: A standard die has six outcomes: 1 through 6. Numbers that are at least 4 are 4, 5, and 6, giving 3 favorable outcomes. Thus, the probability is 3 / 6 = 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Union of Mutually Exclusive Events
prompt: If A and B are mutually exclusive with P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.3, what is P(A ∪ B)?
solution: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together, so P(A ∩ B) = 0. Using the union formula P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), we get 0.4 + 0.3 − 0 = 0.7.

subject: probability
title: Definition of Independence
prompt: Which condition implies independence of events A and B?
options: A and B cannot occur together
solution: Independence is defined by the condition that the joint probability equals the product of the marginal probabilities: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B).

subject: probability
title: Multiplication Rule
prompt: If P(A|B) = 0.2 and P(B) = 0.5, what is P(A ∩ B)?
solution: By the definition of conditional probability, P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B). Rearranging gives P(A ∩ B) = P(A|B) × P(B) = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1.

subject: probability
title: Two Kings With Replacement
prompt: Two cards are drawn with replacement. What is the probability both are Kings?
solution: With replacement, the probability of drawing a King on each draw is 4 / 52. Since the draws are independent, the joint probability is (4 / 52) × (4 / 52) = 16 / 2704 ≈ 0.005917.

subject: probability
title: Intersection from the Union
prompt: If P(A) = 0.65, P(B) = 0.55, and P(A ∪ B) = 0.85, what is P(A ∩ B)?
solution: Using the inclusion–exclusion formula P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), substitute the known values: 0.85 = 0.65 + 0.55 − x. Solving gives x = 0.35.

subject: probability
title: Number of Five-Card Hands
prompt: How many distinct 5-card hands can be drawn from a standard 52-card deck?
solution: A 5-card hand is an unordered selection of 5 cards from 52. The number of such hands is given by the combination formula C(52,5) = 52! / (5!47!) = 2,598,960.

subject: probability
title: Choosing Letters from QUANT
prompt: How many ways can 3 letters be selected from the word 'QUANT' without regard to order?
solution: The word 'QUANT' has 5 distinct letters. Selecting 3 letters without regard to order gives C(5,3) = 5! / (3!2!) = 10.

subject: probability
title: Arranging the Letters of RISK
prompt: How many distinct arrangements of the letters in the word 'RISK' are possible?
solution: The word 'RISK' contains 4 distinct letters. The number of permutations of 4 distinct objects is 4! = 24.

subject: probability
title: Circular Seating Arrangements
prompt: How many ways can 10 people be seated around a round table?
solution: For circular permutations, rotations are considered identical. The number of distinct seatings of n people around a table is (n−1)!. Thus, for 10 people the number is 9! = 362,880.

subject: probability
title: Poker Hands: Exactly One Pair
prompt: How many different 5-card poker hands contain exactly one pair?
solution: Choose the rank for the pair: C(13,1). Choose 2 of the 4 suits for that rank: C(4,2). Choose 3 different ranks from the remaining 12 for the other cards: C(12,3). For each of those 3 ranks choose 1 of 4 suits: 4^3. Total = 13 × 6 × 220 × 64 = 1,098,240.

subject: probability
title: Poker Hands: Full House
prompt: How many different 5-card poker hands are full houses?
solution: Choose the rank for the triple: C(13,1). Choose 3 of its 4 suits: C(4,3). Choose the rank for the pair from remaining 12: C(12,1). Choose 2 of its 4 suits: C(4,2). Total = 13 × 4 × 12 × 6 = 3,744.

subject: probability
title: Birthday Problem
prompt: In a group of 23 people, what is the approximate probability that at least two share the same birthday?
solution: The probability that all 23 birthdays are different is approximately 365/365 × 364/365 × ... × 343/365 ≈ 0.4927. Therefore, the probability that at least two share a birthday is 1 − 0.4927 ≈ 0.5073.

subject: probability
title: Arranging Books on a Shelf
prompt: How many ways can 6 distinct books be arranged on a shelf?
solution: Arranging 6 distinct objects in order is a permutation: 6! = 720.

subject: probability
title: Binary Strings with Three Ones
prompt: How many binary strings of length 8 contain exactly 3 ones?
solution: Choose the positions of the 3 ones from 8 available positions: C(8,3) = 56.

subject: probability
title: Five-Letter Strings with Repetition
prompt: How many distinct 5-letter strings can be formed from the alphabet if letters may repeat?
solution: There are 26 choices for each of the 5 positions. Since repetition is allowed, the total number is 26^5 = 11,881,376.

subject: probability
title: Lattice Paths on a Grid
prompt: How many ways can a rabbit hop from (0,0) to (5,5) moving only right or up?
solution: The rabbit must make 10 moves total: 5 right and 5 up. The number of distinct paths is the number of ways to choose where the 5 right moves occur among 10 positions: C(10,5) = 252.

subject: probability
title: Four-Digit Numbers with Increasing Digits
prompt: How many 4-digit numbers have digits in strictly increasing order?
solution:
A 4-digit number cannot start with 0. If the digits are strictly increasing, 0 could only ever be the first digit, so 0 can never appear.
Choose any 4 distinct digits from $\{1,\dots,9\}$; each choice gives exactly one increasing arrangement:
$$\binom{9}{4} = 126.$$

subject: probability
title: Round-Robin Tournament Games
prompt: In a chess tournament with 8 players, each pair plays exactly once. How many games are played?
solution: Each game corresponds to a unique pair of players. The number of pairs from 8 players is C(8,2) = 28.

subject: probability
title: Six-Letter Words from BALLOON
prompt: How many distinct 6-letter arrangements (words, not necessarily meaningful) can be formed using 6 of the 7 letters of 'BALLOON'?
solution:
BALLOON has letters B, A, L, L, O, O, N. Using 6 of them means leaving out exactly one letter.
- Leave out B, A or N: the remaining 6 letters contain L twice and O twice, giving $\dfrac{6!}{2!\,2!} = 180$ words each, so $3 \times 180 = 540$.
- Leave out one L or one O: the remaining letters have only one repeated pair, giving $\dfrac{6!}{2!} = 360$ words each, so $2 \times 360 = 720$.
These cases give different letter multisets, so they do not overlap. Total $= 540 + 720 = 1260$.

subject: probability
title: Subsets of a Ten-Element Set
prompt: How many subsets does a set of 10 elements have?
solution: Each element can either be included or excluded independently. Therefore, the total number of subsets is 2^10 = 1,024.

subject: probability
title: Arrangements of PROBABILITY
prompt: How many distinct ways can the letters of 'PROBABILITY' be arranged?
solution:
PROBABILITY has 11 letters: P, R, O, B, A, B, I, L, I, T, Y. Both B and I appear twice; all other letters are distinct.
$$\frac{11!}{2!\,2!} = \frac{39{,}916{,}800}{4} = 9{,}979{,}200.$$

subject: probability
title: Stars and Bars: Sharing Candies
prompt: How many ways can 12 identical candies be distributed among 4 children?
solution: This is a stars-and-bars problem: the number of nonnegative integer solutions to x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 = 12 is C(12 + 4 − 1, 4 − 1) = C(15,3) = 455.

subject: probability
title: Choosing a Group of Five
prompt: How many ways can 5 people be chosen from a group of 20?
solution: This is a combination problem: C(20,5) = 20! / (5!15!) = 15,504.

subject: probability
title: Integers Without Repeated Digits
prompt: How many integers from 1 to 1000 inclusive contain no repeated digits?
solution: Counting valid numbers with 1, 2, and 3 digits without repetition yields 9 + 9×9 + 9×9×8 = 9 + 81 + 648 = 738.

subject: probability
title: Phone Numbers Without Repeated Digits
prompt: How many 7-digit phone numbers contain no repeated digits?
solution: The first digit has 10 choices, the second 9, then 8, 7, 6, 5, 4. Multiplying gives 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 = 604,800.

subject: probability
title: Two Heads Given the First Is Heads
prompt: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of exactly two heads given that the first toss was heads?
solution: Given that the first toss is heads, only the remaining two tosses are random. There are four equally likely outcomes for the last two tosses: HH, HT, TH, TT. Exactly one more head must occur to obtain exactly two heads in total, which happens in outcomes HT and TH. Therefore, the probability is 2 / 4 = 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Biased Coin: Two Heads in Three Tosses
prompt: A coin is biased so that P(Heads) = 0.7. What is the probability of getting exactly 2 heads in 3 tosses?
solution: The number of ways to choose which 2 of the 3 tosses are heads is C(3,2) = 3. For each such sequence, the probability is (0.7)^2 × (0.3). Therefore, the total probability is 3 × 0.7^2 × 0.3 = 3 × 0.49 × 0.3 = 0.441.

subject: probability
title: Two Children: At Least One Boy
prompt: Two children are selected at random from a population where boys and girls are equally likely. What is the probability both are boys given that at least one is a boy?
solution: The sample space for two children is {BB, BG, GB, GG}. Given that at least one is a boy, the possible outcomes are {BB, BG, GB}. Only BB satisfies the condition that both are boys. Therefore, the conditional probability is 1 / 3 ≈ 0.333333.

subject: probability
title: Two Red Balls Without Replacement
prompt: A jar contains 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. Two balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability both are red?
solution: The probability the first ball is red is 3 / 5. After removing one red ball, 2 red balls remain out of 4 total balls. Therefore, the probability the second is red is 2 / 4. Multiplying gives (3 / 5) × (2 / 4) = 6 / 20 = 0.3.

subject: probability
title: Bayes: Positive Disease Test
prompt: A test for a disease is 95% accurate: it gives a positive result for 95% of people who have the disease and a negative result for 95% of people who do not. The disease occurs in 1% of the population. What is the probability that a randomly chosen person who tests positive actually has the disease? Give your answer to 3 decimal places.
solution:
Let $D$ be the event that the person has the disease. By Bayes' theorem,
$$P(D\mid +) = \frac{P(+\mid D)P(D)}{P(+\mid D)P(D) + P(+\mid D^c)P(D^c)} = \frac{0.95 \times 0.01}{0.95 \times 0.01 + 0.05 \times 0.99} = \frac{0.0095}{0.059} \approx 0.161.$$

subject: probability
title: Second Die Roll Is Larger
prompt: A fair die is rolled twice. What is the probability the second roll is larger than the first?
solution: There are 36 equally likely ordered pairs. Six of them are ties: (1,1) through (6,6). Of the remaining 30, exactly half have the second roll larger than the first. Thus, the probability is 15 / 36 = 5 / 12 ≈ 0.416667.

subject: probability
title: Fair or Double-Headed Coin
prompt: You have two coins: one fair and one double-headed. You randomly pick one coin and toss it. It comes up heads. What is the probability the coin is double-headed?
solution: Let D be choosing the double-headed coin and F the fair coin. P(D)=P(F)=0.5. P(H|D)=1 and P(H|F)=0.5. By Bayes’ theorem: P(D|H) = [1 × 0.5] / [1 × 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.5] = 0.5 / 0.75 = 2 / 3 ≈ 0.666667.

subject: probability
title: Monty Hall: Switching Doors
prompt: In the Monty Hall problem, after the host opens one goat door, what is the probability of winning the car if you switch?
solution: Initially, the chance your chosen door hides the car is 1/3. The other two doors together have probability 2/3. When the host reveals a goat behind one of them, the full 2/3 probability transfers to the remaining unopened door. Thus, switching yields a win with probability 2 / 3 ≈ 0.666667.

subject: probability
title: At Least One Ace in Two Cards
prompt: Two cards are drawn from a standard 52-card deck without replacement. What is the probability that at least one is an Ace? Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
solution:
Use the complement. The probability that neither card is an Ace is
$$\frac{48}{52} \times \frac{47}{51} = \frac{2256}{2652} \approx 0.8507.$$
So $P(\text{at least one Ace}) = 1 - 0.8507 = \dfrac{396}{2652} = \dfrac{33}{221} \approx 0.1493.$

subject: probability
title: Fair Gambler's Ruin (Start 3, Target 5)
prompt: A gambler starts with \$3 and plays a fair game, winning \$1 with probability 0.5 and losing \$1 with probability 0.5. What is the probability he eventually reaches \$5 before going broke at \$0?
solution: This is a classic gambler’s ruin problem. For a fair game, the probability of reaching the upper boundary N before 0 starting from x is x / N. Here x = 3 and N = 5, so the probability is 3 / 5 = 0.6.

subject: probability
title: Meeting Problem (10-Minute Wait)
prompt: Two people meet at a café at random between 12:00 and 1:00 and each waits 10 minutes. What is the probability they meet?
solution: The meeting region in the unit square corresponds to |x − y| ≤ 1/6. The favorable area is 1 − (5/6)^2 = 1 − 25/36 = 11/36 ≈ 0.305556.

subject: probability
title: First Head on the Fourth Toss
prompt: A fair coin is tossed until the first head appears. What is the probability this takes exactly 4 tosses?
solution: The first 3 tosses must be tails and the 4th must be heads. The probability is (0.5)^3 × 0.5 = (0.5)^4 = 1 / 16 = 0.0625.

subject: probability
title: Sum of Nine Given a Four Shows
prompt: Two dice are rolled. What is the probability the sum is 9 given that at least one die is 4?
solution:
Outcomes with at least one 4: $(4,1),\dots,(4,6)$ and $(1,4),\dots,(6,4)$, with $(4,4)$ counted once, so $6 + 6 - 1 = 11$ equally likely outcomes.
Those summing to 9 are $(4,5)$ and $(5,4)$.
$$P(\text{sum}=9 \mid \text{at least one } 4) = \frac{2}{11} \approx 0.181818.$$

subject: probability
title: Blue After Red Without Replacement
prompt: A jar contains 4 red and 6 blue candies. One candy is drawn. Given that it is red, what is the probability the next candy drawn (without replacement) is blue?
solution: After drawing a red candy, the jar contains 3 red and 6 blue candies, 9 total. The probability the next candy is blue is 6 / 9 = 2 / 3 ≈ 0.666667.

subject: probability
title: Doubling Amoeba Population
prompt: An amoeba population doubles every hour. Starting with 1 amoeba, what is the expected population after 5 hours?
solution: The population doubles each hour, so after n hours the population is 2^n. After 5 hours, the population is 2^5 = 32.

subject: probability
title: Conditioning on an Independent Event
prompt: Two independent events A and B satisfy P(A) = 0.4 and P(B) = 0.5. What is P(A|B)?
solution: For independent events, the occurrence of B does not change the probability of A. Therefore, P(A|B) = P(A) = 0.4.

subject: probability
title: More Heads than Tails in Ten Tosses
prompt: What is the probability that in 10 coin tosses there are more heads than tails?
solution: More heads than tails means at least 6 heads. Compute the binomial sum: Σ_{k=6}^{10} C(10,k)(0.5)^10 = (210 + 120 + 45 + 10 + 1) / 1024 = 386 / 1024 ≈ 0.376953.

subject: probability
title: Two Cards of the Same Suit
prompt: Two cards are drawn without replacement. What is the probability they are of the same suit?
solution: After the first card is drawn, 12 of the remaining 51 cards are of the same suit. Thus, the probability is 12 / 51 ≈ 0.235294.

subject: probability
title: First Two Heads Are Consecutive
prompt: A fair coin is tossed repeatedly. What is the probability that the first two heads occur consecutively?
solution:
Wait for the first head. Whatever happened before it, the next toss is independent and is heads with probability $\tfrac12$.
The first two heads are consecutive exactly when the toss right after the first head is also heads, so the probability is $\tfrac12 = 0.5$.

subject: probability
title: Speeding and Texting: Neither
prompt: If 70% of drivers speed and 40% text while driving, and 25% do both, what is the probability a randomly selected driver does neither?
solution: Let S be speeding and T be texting. P(S ∪ T) = P(S) + P(T) − P(S ∩ T) = 0.7 + 0.4 − 0.25 = 0.85. Therefore, the probability of doing neither is 1 − 0.85 = 0.15.

subject: probability
title: Meeting Problem (15-Minute Wait)
prompt: Two people arrive independently and uniformly between 12:00 and 1:00 and each waits 15 minutes. What is the probability they meet?
solution: Let arrival times x and y be uniform on [0,1]. They meet if |x − y| ≤ 0.25. The total area of the unit square is 1. The area where |x − y| > 0.25 consists of two triangles each with side length 0.75, giving area 2 × (0.75^2 / 2) = 0.5625. Therefore, the meeting probability is 1 − 0.5625 = 0.4375.

subject: probability
title: Poisson Process: Exactly Two Events
prompt: Events occur according to a Poisson process at rate 3 per hour. What is the probability exactly 2 events occur in one hour?
solution: For a Poisson process with rate λ = 3, the probability of k events in time 1 is P(N=2) = e^{−3} × 3^2 / 2! = 9e^{−3} / 2 ≈ 0.224042.

subject: probability
title: Poisson Process Waiting Time
prompt: For a Poisson process with rate 5 per hour, what is the expected waiting time until the next event?
solution: The waiting time in a Poisson process follows an exponential distribution with mean 1/λ. With λ = 5, the expected waiting time is 1 / 5 = 0.2 hours.

subject: probability
title: Broken Stick Triangle
prompt: A stick of length 1 is broken at two points chosen independently and uniformly along its length. What is the probability that the three pieces can form a triangle?
solution:
Let the break points be $U, V \sim \text{U}(0,1)$, with $a = \min(U,V)$ and $b = \max(U,V)$. The pieces have lengths $a$, $b-a$ and $1-b$.
Three lengths summing to 1 form a triangle if and only if each is less than $\tfrac12$:
$$a < \tfrac12, \qquad b - a < \tfrac12, \qquad b > \tfrac12.$$
In the unit square, these conditions cut out two triangles, each of area $\tfrac18$ (one for $U<V$ and one for $V<U$). The total probability is $2 \times \tfrac18 = \tfrac14 = 0.25$.

subject: probability
title: Acute Triangle from Random Points on a Circle
prompt: Three random points are chosen independently and uniformly on the circumference of a circle. What is the probability they form an acute triangle?
solution:
An inscribed triangle is acute if and only if it contains the centre of the circle. This happens exactly when the three points do not all lie in some semicircle.
For $n$ independent uniform points on a circle, $P(\text{all in some semicircle}) = \dfrac{n}{2^{n-1}}$. For $n = 3$ this is $\tfrac34$.
So $P(\text{acute}) = 1 - \tfrac34 = \tfrac14 = 0.25$.

subject: probability
title: Mean of a Uniform Distribution
prompt: A continuous random variable X is uniformly distributed on [2, 8]. What is E[X]?
solution: For a uniform distribution on [a,b], the expected value is (a + b) / 2. Thus, E[X] = (2 + 8) / 2 = 5.

subject: probability
title: Variance of a Uniform Distribution
prompt: A continuous random variable X is uniformly distributed on [2, 8]. What is Var(X)?
solution: For a uniform distribution on [a,b], Var(X) = (b − a)^2 / 12. Here b − a = 6, so Var(X) = 36 / 12 = 3.

subject: probability
title: Variance of a Linear Transformation
prompt: If X ~ N(0, 4), what is Var(2X + 1)?
solution: For a linear transformation aX + b, the variance scales by a^2. Thus, Var(2X + 1) = 2^2 × Var(X) = 4 × 4 = 16.

subject: probability
title: Variance of a Sum of Independent Normals
prompt: If X and Y are independent standard normal variables, what is Var(X + Y)?
solution: For independent variables, Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y). Each has variance 1, so the total variance is 1 + 1 = 2.

subject: probability
title: Variance of a Poisson Variable
prompt: If X ~ Poisson(λ), what is Var(X)?
solution: A fundamental property of the Poisson distribution is that its mean and variance are both equal to λ.

subject: probability
title: Exponential Survival Probability
prompt: The lifetime of a machine follows an exponential distribution with mean 5 years. What is the probability it lasts more than 10 years?
solution: For an exponential distribution with mean 5, the rate is λ = 1 / 5. The survival function is P(T > t) = e^{−λt}. Therefore, P(T > 10) = e^{−(1/5) × 10} = e^{−2} ≈ 0.135335.

subject: probability
title: Normal Standard Deviation
prompt: If X ~ N(10, 9), what is the standard deviation of X?
solution: The variance is 9, so the standard deviation is the square root of the variance: √9 = 3.

subject: probability
title: Minimum of Two Exponentials
prompt: If X and Y are independent exponential random variables with mean 1, what is E[min(X, Y)]?
solution: The minimum of two independent exponential(1) variables is exponential with rate 2, hence mean 1 / 2 = 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Second Moment of a Standard Normal
prompt: If X is normally distributed with mean 0 and variance 1, what is E[X^2]?
solution: For any random variable, Var(X) = E[X^2] − (E[X])^2. Here Var(X) = 1 and E[X] = 0, so E[X^2] = 1.

subject: probability
title: Expected Count in a Poisson Process
prompt: For a Poisson process with rate 4, what is the expected number of events in 3 hours?
solution: The expected number of events in time t is λt. Here λ = 4 and t = 3, so the expectation is 12.

subject: probability
title: Standard Uniform CDF
prompt: If X ~ Uniform(0,1), what is P(X < 0.3)?
solution: For a uniform distribution on [0,1], the probability equals the length of the interval: 0.3 − 0 = 0.3.

subject: probability
title: Mean of an Exponential Distribution
prompt: If X ~ Exp(2), what is E[X]?
solution: The mean of an exponential distribution with rate λ is 1 / λ. Thus, E[X] = 1 / 2 = 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Mean of a Linear Density
prompt: A random variable X has density f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. What is E[X]?
solution: Compute E[X] = ∫₀¹ x · 2x dx = 2 ∫₀¹ x² dx = 2 / 3 ≈ 0.666667.

subject: probability
title: Variance of a Linear Density
prompt: A random variable X has density f(x) = 2x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. What is Var(X)?
solution: First compute E[X] = 2/3 and E[X²] = ∫₀¹ 2x · x² dx = 2 ∫₀¹ x³ dx = 1/2. Then Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])² = 0.5 − (4/9) = 1/18 ≈ 0.055556.

subject: probability
title: Normal Within One Standard Deviation
prompt: If X ~ N(0,1), what is P(|X| < 1)?
solution: For the standard normal distribution, the probability that X lies within one standard deviation of the mean is approximately 0.682689, a well-known property of the normal curve.

subject: probability
title: Expected Value of a Die Roll
prompt: A fair die is rolled. What is the expected value of the outcome?
solution: The expected value of a discrete random variable is the weighted average of all possible outcomes. For a fair die, E[X] = (1+2+3+4+5+6) / 6 = 21 / 6 = 3.5.

subject: probability
title: Expected Sum of Two Dice
prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the expected sum?
solution: The expected value of the sum equals the sum of the expected values. Each die has expectation 3.5, so E[X + Y] = 3.5 + 3.5 = 7.

subject: probability
title: Linearity of Expectation
prompt: If X has E[X] = 2 and Var(X) = 3, what is E[4X − 1]?
solution: Expectation is linear. Therefore, E[4X − 1] = 4E[X] − 1 = 4 × 2 − 1 = 7.

subject: probability
title: Variance Under Scaling and Shift
prompt: If X has Var(X) = 2, what is Var(5X + 3)?
solution: Variance scales with the square of the coefficient: Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X). Thus, Var(5X + 3) = 25 × 2 = 50.

subject: probability
title: Variance of a Correlated Sum
prompt: Two random variables X and Y have Var(X) = 4, Var(Y) = 9, and Cov(X,Y) = 3. What is Var(X + Y)?
solution: Var(X + Y) = Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2Cov(X,Y) = 4 + 9 + 2×3 = 19.

subject: probability
title: Two-Asset Portfolio Variance
prompt: A portfolio consists of two assets with weights 0.5 and 0.5, variances 4 and 16, and covariance 2. What is the portfolio variance?
solution: Portfolio variance is w1²Var1 + w2²Var2 + 2w1w2Cov. Substituting: (0.25×4) + (0.25×16) + (2×0.5×0.5×2) = 1 + 4 + 1 = 6.

subject: probability
title: Expected Payoff of a Bet
prompt: A game pays \$10 with probability 0.2 and loses \$5 otherwise. What is the expected payoff?

subject: probability
title: Expected Tosses Until the First Head
prompt: A fair coin is tossed until the first head appears. What is the expected number of tosses?
solution: This follows a geometric distribution with success probability p = 0.5. The expected number of trials is 1 / p = 2.

subject: probability
title: Zero Covariance vs Independence
prompt: If Cov(X,Y) = 0 and Var(X) and Var(Y) are positive, are X and Y independent?
solution: Zero covariance implies no linear relationship, but it does not imply independence except in special cases such as the joint normal distribution.

subject: probability
title: Variance of a Discrete Uniform
prompt: A random variable X takes values 1, 2, 3 with equal probability. What is Var(X)?

subject: probability
title: Covariance of Independent Dice
prompt: Two independent fair dice are rolled. What is Cov(X,Y)?
solution: For independent variables, covariance is zero: Cov(X,Y) = 0.

subject: probability
title: Covariance from Correlation
prompt: If Corr(X,Y) = 0.5 and Var(X) = 4 and Var(Y) = 9, what is Cov(X,Y)?
solution: Cov(X,Y) = Corr(X,Y) × √Var(X) × √Var(Y) = 0.5 × 2 × 3 = 3.

subject: probability
title: Coupon Collector Problem
prompt: In the coupon collector problem with 10 coupons, what is the expected number of purchases required to collect all coupons?
solution: The expected number is n(1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/n). For n = 10, this is approximately 10 × 2.928968 = 29.29.

subject: probability
title: Mean Squared Deviation About a Point
prompt: A random variable has E[X] = 5 and Var(X) = 4. What is E[(X − 3)²]?

subject: probability
title: Minimum-Variance Hedge Ratio
prompt: A stock and an index have correlation 0.8, stock volatility 20%, index volatility 10%. What is the optimal hedge ratio?
solution: Optimal hedge ratio h = ρ σ_stock / σ_index = 0.8 × 0.20 / 0.10 = 1.6.

subject: probability
title: Expectation of a Product
prompt: Let X and Y be independent with E[X] = 1 and E[Y] = 2. What is E[XY]?
solution: For independent variables, E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] = 1 × 2 = 2.

subject: probability
title: Expected Rolls Until a Six
prompt: A fair die is rolled until a 6 appears. What is the expected number of rolls?
solution: This is a geometric distribution with success probability p = 1/6. The expected number of trials is 1 / p = 6.

subject: probability
title: Variance of a Difference
prompt: Two assets have returns X and Y with Var(X) = 1, Var(Y) = 1, and Cov(X,Y) = −0.5. What is Var(X − Y)?

subject: probability
title: Expectation of a Two-Point Distribution
prompt: A random variable has P(X = 1) = 0.4 and P(X = 3) = 0.6. What is E[X]?

subject: probability
title: Uncorrelated Jointly Normal Variables
prompt: If X and Y are jointly normally distributed and Cov(X,Y) = 0, are they independent?
solution: For jointly normally distributed variables, zero covariance implies independence.

subject: probability
title: Probability of the Sequence HTH
prompt: Three fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of getting the pattern HTH in that order?
solution: Each coin toss is independent with probability 0.5 for heads or tails. The probability of the specific sequence HTH is (0.5)^3 = 1 / 8 = 0.125.

subject: probability
title: First Die Is Larger
prompt: Two dice are rolled. What is the probability the first die is larger than the second?
solution: There are 36 equally likely outcomes. Six outcomes are ties. Of the remaining 30, exactly half have the first die larger. Thus the probability is 15 / 36 = 5 / 12 ≈ 0.416667.

subject: probability
title: Balls Drawn in Increasing Order
prompt: Five balls numbered 1 through 5 are drawn one by one without replacement. What is the probability they appear in increasing order?
solution: All 5! = 120 orders are equally likely. Only one of them is strictly increasing. Thus, the probability is 1 / 120 ≈ 0.008333.

subject: probability
title: HHT Before TTH
prompt: In a sequence of coin tosses, what is the probability that the pattern HHT appears before TTH?
solution: By symmetry of the coin, both patterns are equally likely to appear first. Therefore, the probability is 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Fair Gambler's Ruin (Start 4, Target 6)
prompt: A gambler starts with \$4 and plays a fair game, winning or losing \$1 with equal probability. What is the probability he reaches \$6 before going broke at \$0?
solution: For a fair gambler’s ruin problem, the probability of reaching N before 0 when starting at x is x / N. Here x = 4 and N = 6, so the probability is 4 / 6 = 2 / 3 ≈ 0.666667.

subject: probability
title: Colour of the Last Ball Drawn
prompt: An urn contains 5 red and 5 blue balls. Balls are drawn one at a time without replacement. What is the probability the last ball drawn is red?
solution: By symmetry, each ball is equally likely to be the last drawn. Since 5 of the 10 balls are red, the probability the final ball is red is 5 / 10 = 0.5.

subject: probability
title: Largest of Three Chosen Numbers
prompt: Three distinct numbers are chosen at random from {1,2,3,4,5}. What is the probability the largest number chosen is 5?
solution: The total number of ways to choose 3 numbers from 5 is C(5,3) = 10. The number of selections that include 5 is C(4,2) = 6. Therefore, the probability is 6 / 10 = 0.6.

subject: probability
title: Hypergeometric: Two Reds in Four Draws
prompt: Four balls are drawn from an urn containing 3 red and 5 blue balls. What is the probability exactly two are red?
solution:
Ways to choose exactly two red and two blue: $\binom{3}{2}\binom{5}{2} = 3 \times 10 = 30$.
Total ways to choose 4 balls from 8: $\binom{8}{4} = 70$.
$$P = \frac{30}{70} = \frac{3}{7} \approx 0.428571.$$

subject: probability
title: Maximum of Four Dice
prompt: A fair die is rolled four times. What is the probability the maximum value observed is exactly 4?

subject: probability
title: Higher of Two Cards Is a King
prompt: Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard 52-card deck, with Aces ranked high. What is the probability that the higher-ranked of the two cards is a King? (If both cards are Kings, the higher card counts as a King.) Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
solution:
The higher card is a King exactly when both cards rank King or lower but not both rank Queen or lower:
$$P = \frac{\binom{48}{2} - \binom{44}{2}}{\binom{52}{2}} = \frac{1128 - 946}{1326} = \frac{182}{1326} = \frac{7}{51} \approx 0.1373.$$
Check by cases: one King and one card from 2 to Queen gives $4 \times 44 = 176$ pairs, and two Kings give $\binom42 = 6$ pairs. That is $182$ of $1326$ pairs.

subject: probability
title: Expected Maximum of a Sample
prompt: Five distinct numbers are chosen at random (without replacement) from $\{1, 2, \dots, 20\}$. What is the expected value of the largest number chosen?
solution:
$P(\max = k) = \dbinom{k-1}{4} \big/ \dbinom{20}{5}$ for $k = 5,\dots,20$. So
$$E[\max] = \frac{\sum_{k} k\binom{k-1}{4}}{\binom{20}{5}} = \frac{5\sum_k \binom{k}{5}}{\binom{20}{5}} = \frac{5\binom{21}{6}}{\binom{20}{5}} = \frac{5 \times 21}{6} = 17.5.$$
In general, for a sample of $n$ from $\{1,\dots,N\}$ without replacement, $E[\max] = \dfrac{n(N+1)}{n+1}$. This is exact, not an approximation.

subject: probability
title: Colour Pattern Without Replacement
prompt: Four balls are drawn from an urn containing 6 red and 4 blue balls. What is the probability the colors appear in the pattern RBRB?
solution:
Multiply the conditional probabilities for each draw:
$$P(RBRB) = \frac{6}{10} \times \frac{4}{9} \times \frac{5}{8} \times \frac{3}{7} = \frac{360}{5040} = \frac{1}{14} \approx 0.071429.$$

subject: probability
title: Expected Longest Run of Heads
prompt: A fair coin is tossed 10 times. Let $L$ be the length of the longest run of consecutive heads ($L = 0$ if there are no heads). What is $E[L]$? Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
solution:
Use $E[L] = \sum_{k=1}^{10} P(L \ge k)$. Let $a_k$ be the number of length-10 sequences with no run of $k$ heads. Then $a_k$ satisfies the recursion $a_n = a_{n-1} + \dots + a_{n-k}$, which gives
$a_1 = 1,\ a_2 = 144,\ a_3 = 504,\ a_4 = 773,\ a_5 = 912,\ a_6 = 976,\ a_7 = 1004,\ a_8 = 1016,\ a_9 = 1021,\ a_{10} = 1023.$
So the counts with $L \ge k$ are $1024 - a_k$: $1023, 880, 520, 251, 112, 48, 20, 8, 3, 1$, which sum to $2866$.
$$E[L] = \frac{2866}{1024} = \frac{1433}{512} \approx 2.7988.$$

subject: probability
title: Median of Three Uniforms
prompt: What is the probability that the median of three independent uniform(0,1) variables exceeds 0.5?
solution: By symmetry of the uniform distribution, the median is equally likely to be above or below 0.5. Hence the probability is 0.5.

subject: probability
title: All Three Colours Drawn
prompt: Three balls are drawn from an urn containing 4 red, 3 blue, and 3 green balls. What is the probability all three colors appear?
solution:
Favourable: one ball of each colour, $\binom41\binom31\binom31 = 36$ ways.
Total: $\binom{10}{3} = 120$ ways.
$$P = \frac{36}{120} = 0.3.$$

subject: probability
title: Expected Wait for HT
prompt: A fair coin is tossed until the pattern HT appears. What is the expected number of tosses?
solution: Using pattern waiting time theory, the expected time for HT is 1 / (P(H)P(T)) = 1 / (0.5 × 0.5) = 4.

subject: probability
title: Smallest Selected Number
prompt: Five numbers are selected from {1,...,10}. What is the probability the smallest selected number is 3?
solution:
The smallest number is 3 exactly when 3 is chosen, 1 and 2 are not, and the other four numbers come from $\{4,\dots,10\}$ (7 numbers).
Favourable: $\binom{7}{4} = 35$. Total: $\binom{10}{5} = 252$.
$$P = \frac{35}{252} = \frac{5}{36} \approx 0.138889.$$

subject: probability
title: Three Dice in Strictly Increasing Order
prompt: Three fair dice are rolled. What is the probability their values are in strictly increasing order?
solution:
A strictly increasing outcome is determined by choosing 3 distinct values from 6; each set has exactly one increasing order:
$$P = \frac{\binom{6}{3}}{6^3} = \frac{20}{216} \approx 0.092593.$$
Equivalently, $P(\text{all distinct}) \times \tfrac{1}{3!} = \tfrac{120}{216} \times \tfrac16 = \tfrac{20}{216}$.

subject: probability
title: Draws Until a Colour Is Exhausted
prompt: An urn contains 5 white and 5 black balls. Balls are drawn one at a time without replacement until all balls of one colour have been drawn. What is the expected number of draws? Give your answer to 4 decimal places.
solution:
When one colour is exhausted, the balls left in the urn are all of the other colour. So the number of draws is $D = 10 - R$, where $R$ is the number of balls left.
A particular white ball is left over exactly when it comes after all 5 black balls in the random order. Among those 6 balls it is last with probability $\tfrac16$. The same holds for each black ball relative to the 5 whites.
By linearity, $E[R] = 10 \times \tfrac16 = \tfrac53$, so
$$E[D] = 10 - \frac53 = \frac{25}{3} \approx 8.3333.$$

subject: probability
title: Relative Order in a Random Permutation
prompt: What is the probability that in a random permutation of {1,...,6}, the number 6 appears after 5?
solution: In a random permutation, the relative order of any two numbers is equally likely. Thus the probability that 6 appears after 5 is 1 / 2.
